newsitem.title: USA: Future looks bright for Latin American economies.
newsitem.headline: Future looks bright for Latin American economies.

text.p: Buoyed by powerful indications of recovery, Latin American officials sent a clear message on Sunday about their economies -- growth is back and better than ever.

The finance ministers from Brazil, Mexico and Argentina assured audiences gathered for the International Monetary Fund and World Bank annual meetings that the perils of last year's financial meltdown have passed and the time has come for higher economic growth.

"It's clear that economic recovery is on the way," Mexican Secretary of Finance Guillermo Ortiz said at a panel sponsored by the Institute of International Finance (IIF). "Industrial production has already reached pre-crisis levels."
Mexico's path back from last year's recession, when the economy contracted 6.9 percent, was paved with strong export growth, as firms took advantage of the weak peso to gain access to U.S. markets.
"Is export growth sustainable?" Ortiz asked Sunday. "We think it is."

Mexico astounded observers in August by posting stunning 7.2 percent growth year-over-year in the second quarter, confirming that the country had rebounded from the currency crisis that rocked world markets.

The crisis in Latin America began in December 1994 when Mexico botched an attempt to devalue its peso and sparked international investor panic that sent international investors fleeing from emerging market assets.
With the help of the U.S.-sponsored bailout, Mexico recovered from its worst recession in decades, while Argentina and Brazil rode out the storm by sticking to their economic stabilisation plans.

Latin policymakers insisted that, despite the last year's instability, their economies have emerged healthier from the crisis, with lower inflation and increased reserves laying the groundwork for sustained expansion into the future.

Argentine Economy Minister Roque Fernandez said his country's economy was emerging from recession, as the government projects gross domestic product will expand by 5.0 percent in 1997, up from an estimated 3.5 percent this year.
"There is no doubt the economy is moving at a very good pace out of the recession," Fernandez said.
Argentina still must struggle to bring down its soaring 17 percent unemployment, but the increasing levels of industrial investment provided evidence the economy is on track, he said.

Brazil, with the largest GDP and population in Latin America, should emerge from its slowdown this year to thrive as the government further opens the economy, according to Finance Minister Pedro Malan.
"We are creating the conditions for higher sustainable growth over time," he said at an IIF panel.

Because of privatisation, increased productivity and, most important, the taming of inflation, Brazil is poised to grow 4.5 percent next year compared to an estimated three percent this year, Malan said.

As international investment to Latin America reached record levels in 1996, the ministers assured policymakers and investors that this time the Mexican, Brazilian and Argentine economic recoveries are built on solid foundations.
